A cross-city research project

Green Stormwater Infrastructure Maintenance

We are a research team from the University of Toronto's Department of Geography & Planning investigating how green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) is maintained across four North American cities.

Funded by an Insight Development Grant from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC).

Our four study cities

Two Canadian and two U.S. cities, each with its own approach to maintaining green stormwater infrastructure.

Portland Toronto Vancouver Washington, DC

About Green Stormwater Infrastructure

Green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) uses plants, soil, and other natural features to manage rain where it falls. Instead of rushing into sewers, runoff from streets and rooftops is captured, slowed down, and soaked into the ground. Common types include:

  • – shallow planted areas that collect and soak up runoff
  • – planted channels along streets that slow and filter stormwater
  • – street trees planted over underground space that stores runoff
  • – rooftops covered in plants that absorb rain before it reaches the ground
  • – pavement that lets water pass through into the soil below

Why it matters

Reduces flooding

Soaks up rain where it falls, easing pressure on sewers during heavy storms.

Greener, healthier streets

Adds shade, cleaner water, and habitat for plants and pollinators.

Only works if it is maintained

Clogged inlets and dying plants stop GSI from doing its job, so long-term care is essential.

Creates jobs and advances equity

Maintenance work can build green jobs and community capacity, and reduce environmental inequities.

Methodology

We aim to better understand GSI maintenance systems by exploring:

  • How cities partner with organizations to maintain GSI assets
  • What maintenance looks like by asset type, season, and location — and who does the work
  • How maintenance labor is resourced, valued, and whether equity or justice frameworks guide this work
  • Where gaps in coverage exist, and how these map onto social and spatial inequalities

We are conducting interviews with community members, planners, and program managers to understand how GSI maintenance programs contribute to social and environmental justice in diverse neighbourhoods across each city.

Interested in being involved?

We want to hear from people in Portland, Toronto, Vancouver, and Washington, DC, whether or not you know anything about green stormwater infrastructure. No experience needed.

We're interviewing:

  • Residents
  • Community leaders
  • Volunteer groups
  • Maintenance workers
  • Crew leads
  • Organization leaders
  • Urban planners
  • Anyone else who works with GSI
